title: Easton's Theorem and Cardinal Invariants of the Continuum

items.title: Necessary constraints on the regular-cardinal continuum function
items.statement: In ZFC, the function κ ↦ 2^κ on infinite regular cardinals satisfies κ < 2^κ, monotonicity, and cf(2^κ)>κ.
items.strategy: Cantor gives strictness; injection of power sets gives monotonicity; apply the published König corollary for the cofinality bound. AC identifies cardinal values and is spent in the König corollary.

items.title: Easton functions on regular cardinals
items.statement: An Easton function F on a set or definable class of infinite regular cardinals has cardinal values, is nondecreasing, and satisfies cf(F(κ))>κ; the latter implies F(κ)>κ. A class version is understood over a two-sorted class theory with F among its classes.

items.title: The Easton-support product of higher Cohen forcings
items.statement: For an Easton function F, a condition in P(F) is a set-sized partial map on triples (κ,α,β), κ in dom F, α<κ, β<F(κ), with bit values and fewer than γ triples with first coordinate at most γ for every infinite regular γ. Stronger conditions extend functions. Initial segments P≤λ and tails P>λ split by their first coordinate.
items.axiom_base: ZF set-length definition; GBC for the class version

items.title: Set-length Easton-support forcing iterations
items.statement: A set-length Easton-support iteration has the same successor two-step rule as an ordinary forcing iteration and, at a limit δ, a coherent condition whose non-top support below each infinite regular γ≤δ has size <γ. It is a different presentation from the ground-model product; no equivalence is asserted by definition.
items.axiom_base: ZF set-length definition; GBC for the class version

items.title: Easton head chain condition and tail closure
items.statement: Assume GCH. For every infinite regular λ, P≤λ has the λ⁺-chain condition and P>λ is λ⁺-closed. The factorization P≅P≤λ×P>λ holds for set products and for set conditions in the class product.
items.axiom_base: ZFC+GCH for set products; GBC+Global Choice+GCH for class-condition clause
items.strategy: The Easton support bound makes each head domain smaller than λ. Apply the published generalized delta-system lemma to λ⁺ heads, thin to equal bit assignments on the root, and unite two compatible conditions. A decreasing tail chain of length at most λ has a union respecting every regular coordinate γ>λ by regularity. AC chooses the thinning and lower bounds.

items.title: A closed Easton tail adds no short sequences across its chain-condition head
items.statement: In ZFC, if set forcing P is λ⁺-closed and set forcing Q is λ⁺-cc, then in a P×Q extension every function λ→V belongs to the intermediate Q extension.
items.strategy: For each coordinate α<λ, recursively build a maximal Q-antichain of value decisions while descending in P; λ⁺-cc stops before λ⁺, and P closure supplies a lower bound. Intersect the λ dense sets of such P conditions using closure; the Q generic then selects the value at each α. AC chooses the antichains and decisions. This is Jech Lemma 15.19 with the library’s strict closure convention translated to λ⁺-closed.

items.title: Set-sized Easton forcing preserves cardinals and cofinalities
items.statement: Over ZFC+GCH, the set-sized Easton product P(F) preserves every ground-model cardinal and cofinality.
items.strategy: If a regular ground cardinal θ first lost regularity, a cofinal map from some regular λ<θ into θ would already be in the P≤λ extension by the tail/head lemma. P≤λ is λ⁺-cc and hence θ-cc, contradicting the published chain-condition preservation theorem. Preserving all regular cardinals then preserves cardinals and cofinalities. AC is used in the two supplier lemmas.

items.title: GCH counts Easton head conditions and subset names
items.statement: Assume GCH, κ is regular in dom F, and cf(F(κ))>κ. Then |P≤κ|=F(κ), and there are at most F(κ) nice P≤κ-names for subsets of κ.
items.strategy: First prove under GCH that λ^κ=λ whenever λ≥κ⁺ and cf λ>κ: for successor λ=μ⁺, bound by (2^μ)^κ=2^μ; for limit λ, every κ-sequence is bounded below λ, then induct. Put λ=F(κ). Head conditions have <κ-sized domains in κ×λ, hence λ many possibilities; the κ-coordinate supplies λ distinct ones. For each α<κ, choose a maximal antichain deciding α-membership in an arbitrary subset name and retain its positive members; the usual density argument proves equality with this nice name. Each antichain has at most κ members, so code κ many antichains by λ^κ=λ. AC is used for cardinal codes and maximal antichains.

items.title: Set-sized Easton realization on regular cardinals
items.statement: Over ZFC+GCH, forcing with a set-sized Easton product P(F) yields 2^κ=F(κ) for every κ in dom F while preserving cardinals and cofinalities.
items.strategy: For each β<F(κ), dense coordinate decisions yield a total κ-bit real; a fresh coordinate separates distinct β, giving the lower bound. The tail adds no κ-sequences; every subset of κ comes from P≤κ and the nice-name bound gives the upper bound. The preservation theorem keeps F(κ) a cardinal. AC is used in name selection.

items.title: Class-theoretic ground assumptions for Easton forcing
items.statement: For this page, a GBC+Global Choice ground is a two-sorted model of first-order Gödel–Bernays class theory with set-level ZFC, class comprehension for formulas quantifying only over sets (with set and class parameters), class Replacement for set-indexed class functions, and a class well-order of all sets. GCH is an additional set-theoretic hypothesis. A definable Easton class function and the Easton product are classes in this ground; genericity means meeting every dense class in the ground-model class part.

references.title: Jech, Set Theory, Chapter 15, class forcing discussion, printed pp.235–237
Jech, Set Theory, Chapter 15, Theorem 15.18 and class-forcing proof, printed pp. 233–237

items.title: Set-stage names and the forcing truth lemma for the Easton class product
items.statement: Let M be a countable transitive GBC+Global Choice+GCH model, F a definable Easton class function, and G generic for the Easton class product P(F) over all dense classes of M. Every set name lies in some set initial segment, M[G]=⋃_{λ regular}M[G≤λ], and for each fixed first-order formula the class forcing relation is definable in M and satisfies the truth lemma.
items.strategy: For regular λ<μ, P≤μ=P≤λ×P(λ,μ], so the inclusion is a complete embedding of the set Boolean completions; atomic Boolean values of names already in Bλ are unchanged at larger stages. Every name is a set and the ranks/coordinates in its transitive closure have an ordinal bound, hence it is a Bλ-name for some regular λ. Define atomic forcing by the stable set-stage Boolean values. For each fixed formula, recurse on syntax: p forces negation when no stronger condition forces the subformula; p forces an existential when below p it is dense to find a stronger condition and a set name witnessing the subformula. Each clause is first-order definable with class parameters P,F in GBC, because the formula is fixed and all quantified conditions/names are sets; no class-sized join is invoked. The deciding class is dense by the negation clause. Induct on formulas to prove truth: in the existential case a true witness has a set name, and a condition in G forces its matrix by induction; conversely G meets the definable dense witness class. The countable external model permits an M-generic meeting its countably many represented dense classes. Stage valuation agrees under complete embeddings, giving the asserted union. Global Choice supplies uniform class choices where needed; this is the exact class-forcing interface sketched by Jech pp.235–236.

references.title: Jech, Set Theory, Chapter 15, Theorem 15.18 and class-forcing proof, printed pp. 233–237

items.title: Uniform head-antichain decisions below a class tail
items.statement: Fix a regular λ, a first-order formula φ, and a ground set sequence of at most λ tuples of Easton set names. In a class-generic extension there is one generic tail condition and a ground set of maximal P≤λ antichains which decide φ on every tuple; true existential decisions carry set-name witnesses. Consequently formula-defined truth values on a ground set of at most λ candidate names form a set already in M[G≤λ].
items.strategy: Write P=P≤λ×P>λ. For each tuple indexed by α, let Dα be the class of tail conditions t for which a maximal head antichain Wα has been assigned a truth decision for φ under t∪q for every q∈Wα; if the decided formula is existential and true, assign a witnessing set name. Dα is dense: starting below any t, recursively choose a head condition incompatible with previous cells, strengthen the tail and head to decide φ, and choose a witness when appropriate. At every limit of length at most λ, unite the descending tail conditions; the Easton tail is closed under such unions. A run of λ+ incompatible head cells is impossible by the λ+-cc, so the recursion stops with a maximal antichain of at most λ cells and a common tail lower bound. For at most λ indices, recursively meet their Dα and take the tail union, forming a definable dense class D; G meets D. Global Choice and class Replacement collect the indexed antichains, decisions and witness names into ground sets. The head generic meets each maximal Wα in one cell, so the class forcing truth lemma identifies its assigned decision with the actual truth value. The resulting set of true indices is defined in the ordinary set-forcing stage M[G≤λ]. This is the formula-decision version of Jech Lemma 15.19 and the class-tail argument on printed pp.236–237.

references.title: Jech, Set Theory, Chapter 15, Theorem 15.18 and class-forcing proof, printed pp. 233–237

items.title: Separation and Power Set in the Easton class extension
items.statement: Under the Easton class-generic hypotheses, M[G] satisfies the Separation and Power Set schemes; for every set a∈M[G], its full power set in M[G] already belongs to one suitable set-stage extension M[G≤λ].
items.strategy: Choose a set name τ for a and a regular λ above its stage and above the ground cardinality of dom(τ). Enumerate the candidate member names in dom(τ) by a ground ordinal μ<λ. For any fixed formula ψ(x,parameters), enlarge λ to contain the parameter names and apply the uniform head-antichain decision lemma to the μ fixed instances σ_α∈τ and ψ(σ_α,parameters). One generic tail condition yields ground-set head antichains deciding every instance; in M[G≤λ], use its generic head and ordinary set Separation/Replacement on the μ-indexed decisions to form precisely {σ_α^G∈a:ψ(σ_α^G)}. The class truth lemma identifies these decisions with M[G]-truth, proving Separation without assuming the subset already exists. For Power Set, any b⊆a in M[G] belongs to some later set stage M[G≤γ]. The μ-bit membership code α↦[σ_α^G∈b] is a sequence in that set-stage extension. The factor P≤γ=P≤λ×P(λ,γ] has λ+-cc head and λ+-closed tail, so the set-product no-new-short-sequences lemma puts this μ-code in M[G≤λ]. Reconstruct b from the code and the candidate names in the head stage. Thus every subset of a belongs to M[G≤λ], and its complete power set is the head-stage power set of a. This fills the Separation step Jech leaves implicit on printed p.236.

references.title: Jech, Set Theory, Chapter 15, Theorem 15.18 and class-forcing proof, printed pp. 233–237

items.title: Replacement in the Easton class extension
items.statement: Under the Easton class-generic hypotheses, M[G] satisfies the Replacement scheme for every fixed first-order formula with set parameters.
items.strategy: Let a=τ^G and suppose ψ(x,y,parameters) defines exactly one y for each x∈a in M[G]. Take λ regular above all parameter-name stages and above |dom(τ)| in M, and enumerate the candidate member names σ_α, α<μ<λ. By the class truth lemma choose a condition in G forcing the functional assertion, then work below it. For each α, the dense class of conditions decides σ_α∈τ; on the true branch it also decides the existential ψ(σ_α,y) and supplies a witness set name ρ. Apply the uniform tail/head decision lemma, below the chosen condition, to obtain one tail condition and a ground set of head antichains with all branch decisions and witness names. Their union S is a ground set of names, hence all of S lies in one Bγ and {ρ^G:ρ∈S} is a set in M[G≤γ]. Every actual value of ψ on a is in that set by the truth lemma. The already established Separation scheme cuts out exactly {y:∃x∈a ψ(x,y)}, proving Replacement. Global Choice is used to select the indexed head cells and witness names. This expands Jech printed pp.236–237 without assuming that a class-sized image is already a set.

items.title: The Easton class-generic union satisfies ZFC
items.statement: Over a countable transitive GBC+Global Choice+GCH model with definable class Easton function F, an Easton-class-generic G yields M[G]=⋃λ M[G≤λ], satisfies the forcing truth lemma and all ZFC axioms, and has the same subsets of each ordinal λ as a suitable set-stage extension.
items.strategy: The class-forcing truth lemma gives definable forcing for fixed formulas and the union of nested set-stage extensions. The local head-decision lemma and its applications establish Separation, Power Set and Replacement without treating a proper class of truth values as a set. Extensionality, Foundation, Infinity, Pairing, Union and Choice hold because each finite set of parameters and its ordinary set constructions lie in some transitive set-forcing stage M[G≤λ], and set-stage Choice supplies a well-order of each set. The class-tail/head reduction puts every subset of an ordinal λ into a sufficiently large set-stage extension. Therefore M[G] satisfies ZFC and has the claimed set-stage boundedness. Global Choice is used only in the ground class construction and uniform witness/antichain selections; ordinary AC in the extension comes from set-stage Choice.

items.title: Easton’s theorem for regular cardinals
items.statement: For a definable Easton class function F with domain all infinite regular cardinals over a countable transitive GBC+Global Choice+GCH ground model, the Easton class product has a generic extension satisfying ZFC with the same cardinals and cofinalities and 2^κ=F(κ) at every infinite regular κ. Consequently these are the only ZFC constraints on regular-cardinal values in the corresponding relative-consistency construction.
items.strategy: By the class-generic-model lemma, M[G] satisfies ZFC. For each regular λ, factor P into the set head P≤λ and class tail P>λ. Every subset of λ in M[G] appears at a later set stage, and the set-product no-new-short-sequences lemma moves its λ-bit code into M[G≤λ]. The set-sized Easton realization theorem computes exactly F(λ) subsets of λ in that head, so 2^λ=F(λ) in the class extension. If a ground regular κ became singular, choose a new cofinal map f:μ→κ with μ<κ regular already in M (regularity cannot increase). The tail beyond μ adds no μ-sequence over M[G≤μ], while the μ+-cc head preserves κ, a contradiction. All regular ground cardinals remain regular. A collapsed singular cardinal would collapse a regular cardinal strictly between its new size and its old value. For an arbitrary ordinal δ of ground cofinality κ, a new shorter cofinal sequence in δ pulls back along a ground increasing cofinal κ-sequence to a shorter cofinal sequence in κ; thus all ordinal cofinalities are preserved as well. To formulate relative consistency from ZFC, pass to a constructible GCH ground and use a definable Easton prescription there; arbitrary external class prescriptions are not claimed to be ZFC formulas. GC/AC uses are inherited from the local class and set forcing lemmas.

items.title: Easton’s theorem does not prescribe singular-cardinal powers
items.statement: The Easton realization statement addresses regular cardinals. At a singular κ, monotonicity from lower cardinals and the König bound cf(2^κ)>κ still hold; this page makes no independent assignment of 2^κ and does not infer singular values from arbitrary regular prescriptions.

items.title: Almost inclusion, pseudointersections and towers
items.statement: For infinite A,B⊆ω write A⊆*B when A\B is finite. The quotient Boolean algebra P(ω)/fin identifies sets modulo finite symmetric difference; its positive forcing consists of [ω]^ω modulo finite, with p stronger than q exactly when p⊆*q. Some sources display the reverse, weaker-than relation as ⊇*. A pseudointersection of F⊆[ω]^ω is an infinite X⊆ω with X⊆*A for every A∈F. F has the strong finite-intersection property when each finite intersection is infinite. A tower is a ⊇*-well-ordered family with no pseudointersection; repeat representatives may be removed.

items.title: A tower of size at most the continuum exists
items.statement: In ZFC, there is a tower of infinite subsets of ω whose length is at most c=2^ℵ0.
items.strategy: Well-order [ω]^ω as (X_α:α<c). Recursively maintain a strictly ⊇*-descending family. At stage α, if it has no pseudointersection, stop. Otherwise choose an infinite pseudointersection Y, split Y into two infinite pieces and choose a piece A_α for which X_α is not almost included in A_α. This A_α is almost contained in every earlier member. If the recursion lasts c stages, every X_α has been excluded as a pseudointersection; thus it is a tower. AC supplies the well-order and stagewise choices.

items.title: The pseudointersection and tower numbers
items.statement: In ZFC, p is the least size of a strong-finite-intersection family with no pseudointersection; t is the least length of a tower. Both minima exist because the preceding lemma supplies a tower, which also has the strong finite-intersection property, and AC well-orders the candidate sizes.

items.title: Basic bounds for p and t
items.statement: In ZFC, ℵ1≤p≤t≤c; every countable strong-finite-intersection family and every countable descending family has a pseudointersection.
items.strategy: For a countable SFIP family take finite intersections B_n and choose strictly increasing x_n∈B_n; its range is a pseudointersection. Thus p≥ℵ1, and because every tower has SFIP, t≥ℵ1 and p≤t. The preceding tower-existence lemma gives t≤c. AC supplies the well-orderings and recursive choices.

items.title: Eventual domination and b and d
items.statement: For f,g∈ω^ω, f≤*g means f(n)≤g(n) eventually. The bounding number b is the least size of a ≤*-unbounded family, and the dominating number d is the least size of a ≤*-cofinal family. These are cardinal minima in ZFC.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.title: Basic bounding and dominating relations
items.statement: In ZFC, ℵ1≤b=cf(b)≤cf(d)≤d≤c.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: A diagonal pointwise maximum bounds any countable family. If an unbounded family of size b were a union of fewer than b smaller bounded families, the corresponding bounds would have a common bound; hence b is regular. Partition a dominating family into cf(d) nondominating pieces, choose one witness per piece and bound them if cf(d)<b to contradict domination. AC supplies the cardinal-indexed partitions and witnesses.

items.title: Splitting and reaping numbers
items.statement: S⊆[ω]^ω is splitting if every infinite X⊆ω has some S∈S with X∩S and X\S both infinite; s is the least size of such a family. R⊆[ω]^ω is unreaped if no one set splits every member of R; r is its least size.

items.title: Splitting and reaping comparisons with b and d
items.statement: In ZFC, ℵ1≤s≤d≤c and ℵ1≤b≤r≤c.
items.strategy: For countably many candidate splitters choose nested infinite sides and diagonalize to an infinite set almost contained in the chosen side of each; hence s>ω. Given a countable family R, choose at stage n two fresh points of each of its first n members, put one in a common set and one outside; hence r>ω. For an interval partition P, let φ(P) be the union of its even blocks. For infinite X, let ψ(X) have successive finite blocks ending just after the next X-point. Say P almost dominates Q if every sufficiently late P-block contains an entire Q-block. If P almost dominates ψ(X), every sufficiently late P-block meets X, so φ(P) splits X (Monk Lemma 15). Monk Theorem 13(iii) gives d many P that almost dominate every Q, proving s≤d. If |R|<b, Monk Theorem 13(iv) supplies one P almost dominating every ψ(X), X∈R, so φ(P) splits the whole R and proves b≤r by contraposition. For clarity, Theorem 13(i) constructs a dominating P from a function g by bounding the next-two-endpoint function of Q, and 13(ii) recovers an eventual function bound from an almost-dominating P; these establish the required partition orientation. Theorem 16's printed reference to Lemma 14 is a numbering error: the splitter implication is Lemma 15. AC selects the cardinal witness families; the diagonal arguments themselves use only countable choice available in ZFC.

items.title: Add, cov, non and cof for null and meagre ideals
items.statement: For I equal to the Lebesgue-null ideal N or meagre ideal M on the real line, define add(I) as the least size of an I-family with union outside I, cov(I) as the least size of an I-cover, non(I) as the least size of a set outside I, and cof(I) as the least size of an inclusion-cofinal I-family. All four are evaluated in ZFC.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.title: Elementary bounds on ideal cardinal invariants
items.statement: For I=N or M in ZFC, ℵ1≤add(I)≤min(cov(I),non(I))≤max(cov(I),non(I))≤cof(I)≤c.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: Use the published meagre sigma-ideal theorem under Countable Choice (provided by AC) and the published null sigma-ideal theorem in complete Lebesgue measure for the countable-union lower bound. Any I-cover has union outside I, proving add≤cov. A non-I set is a union of its singleton members, proving add≤non. A cofinal family covers all singletons, giving cov≤cof. For each cofinal basis member B choose x_B outside B; the set of chosen points is outside I, since any I cover would be contained in some B and contain its own excluded x_B. Hence non≤cof. To obtain cof≤c locally, cover each null set by open sets of arbitrarily small measure and intersect their unions to get a null Borel Gδ hull; cover each meagre set by countably many closed nowhere-dense sets to get a meagre Borel Fσ hull. A countable topological basis and measure codes give at most c such Borel hulls. AC selects covers, codes and cardinal minima.

items.title: The fair-coin Borel measure on Cantor space
items.statement: In ZFC, Cantor space 2^ω with its product topology carries a Borel probability measure μ for which every basic cylinder [s], s∈2^n, has μ([s])=2^-n.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: Map x∈[0,1) to its canonical binary sequence, using the expansion eventually zero at dyadic rationals. The inverse image of a length-n cylinder is its corresponding half-open dyadic interval, so this digit map is Borel measurable because cylinders generate the product Borel sigma-algebra. Push forward one-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1). Countable additivity and total mass one come from the published measure; the published interval-measure theorem gives μ([s])=2^-n. No infinite-product extension theorem is needed.

items.title: Borel master codes for null and meagre sets
items.statement: Work in Cantor space 2^ω with its product topology and fair-coin product measure μ, so a basic cylinder [s] has μ([s])=2^-|s|. A null master code is a sequence of clopen sets U_n with μ(U_n)≤2^-n, representing the null limsup ⋂_m⋃_{n≥m}U_n. A meagre master code is a sequence of dense open sets V_n coded by a fixed clopen basis, representing the meagre complement of ⋂_n V_n. The slalom order C consists of finite S(n)⊆ω with Σ_n|S(n)|/2^n finite, ordered by eventual inclusion. Transfer between Cantor space and the real line requires separate measure and category maps.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category
Bartoszyński, Invariants of Measure and Category, Lemmas 3.2–3.9, printed pp.4–7

items.title: Borel-coded small open hulls for null sections
items.statement: Assuming AC, for a Borel H⊂2^ω×2^ω and every positive rational ε, there is a Borel map x↦O_x into codes for open subsets of 2^ω such that H_x⊂O_x and μ(O_x\H_x)<ε. In particular, if every H_x is null, the open hulls can have μ(O_x)<ε.
items.strategy: First prove x↦μ(B_x) is Borel for every Borel B⊂2^ω×2^ω: rectangles have this property, and the class of such B is a monotone class by continuity of the finite measure, so the monotone-class theorem gives all Borel sets. Now induct on a Borel code for H. An open product set has Borel-coded open sections by its countable basic-rectangle decomposition. For a countable union H=∪H_i, give each H_i an open hull with excess <ε/2^(i+1) and take their union; the excess is <ε. At a complement/intersection node write H=∩_n A_n with A_n decreasing and of lower additive Borel rank. Construct Borel-coded open O_n(x)⊃(A_n)_x with μ(O_n(x)\(A_n)_x)<ε/2. Let K_n={x:μ(((A_n)\H)_x)<ε/2}; the section-measure result makes K_n Borel, and K_n increases to all parameters by continuity from above. The least n with x∈K_n is Borel, and O_x=O_n(x) has excess <ε. The countable Borel-code recursion covers every Borel rank; its maps stay Borel through countable union and least-index selection. For null sections, μ(H_x)=0, so the claimed small total measure follows. This supplies the missing constructive content behind Bartoszyński Lemma 3.8.

references.title: Bartoszyński, Invariants of Measure and Category, Lemmas 3.2–3.9, printed pp.4–7

items.title: Borel-coded nowhere-dense covers for meagre sections
items.statement: If H⊂2^ω×2^ω is Borel and every vertical section H_x is meagre, there is a sequence of Borel maps x↦F_n(x) into codes for closed nowhere-dense subsets of 2^ω such that H_x⊂⋃_n F_n(x) for every x.
items.strategy: Prove the stronger uniform Baire-property assertion by induction on a Borel code: for every Borel H there is a Borel open-section code O_x and countably many Borel closed nowhere-dense-section codes F_n(x) with H_x symmetric-difference O_x contained in ∪F_n(x). For an open H use O_x=H_x from its countable product-basis representation and no F_n. Countable unions preserve the assertion by taking unions of open codes and listing all error codes. For a complement replace O_x by 2^ω\cl(O_x), and append boundary(O_x)=cl(O_x)\O_x to the error list; the boundary is closed nowhere dense. All these section codes depend Borelly on x: for a basic cylinder [s], intersection with an open-coded O_x is a countable test, and [s]⊂O_x is a finite-subcover test by compactness. The boundary-hit predicate is Borel because [s] meets the boundary iff the finitely branching tree of extensions t⊇s with [t] meeting O_x but not contained in O_x has nodes at arbitrarily large levels (König). This also codes the new open complement Borelly. If H_x is meagre, then O_x is meagre as well because its symmetric difference with H_x is meagre. A nonempty open subset of Cantor space cannot be meagre: recursively choose the least binary subcylinder inside it avoiding the nth closed nowhere-dense set; the nested cylinders determine a point. This uses no choice principle, so O_x=∅ and the F_n(x) cover H_x. This fills the uniform section step of Bartoszyński Lemma 3.9 without a pointwise AC selection.

items.title: Borel master codes are cofinal in both ideals
items.statement: The meagre master family is inclusion-cofinal and meagre Borel sections have uniform Borel master codes. Assuming AC, the null master family is inclusion-cofinal and null Borel sections have uniform Borel master codes; these are the uniform code maps used in the Cichoń reductions.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: Null sections: apply the uniform-open-hulls lemma to a Borel H with null fibres for open O_j(x)⊃H_x of measure <2^(-j-2). For each x and j, take the canonical prefix-free decomposition of O_j(x) into clopen cylinders; its membership tests and codes are Borel in x. Enumerate all these cylinders in a fixed diagonal order, allowing empty slots; their total measure is finite. Let T_k(x) be the Borel tail sum of their measures and choose Borel least increasing cutoffs h_n(x) with T_{h_n}(x)≤2^-n. Group the finitely many cylinders in [h_n,h_(n+1)) into one clopen C_n(x), so μ(C_n(x))≤2^-n. Each y∈H_x belongs to one cylinder from every O_j(x), hence to infinitely many distinct C_n(x); thus H_x lies in the null limsup code. Conversely summability makes every such limsup null. Meagre sections: use the uniform-closed-covers lemma to obtain Borel closed nowhere-dense codes F_j(x) covering H_x. For each n enumerate the finite interval cylinders S_n,m specifying bits on [n,k), k>n. For any dense open U, one S_n,m lies inside U: process the finitely many 2^n prefixes, extending a common suffix within U one prefix at a time. Every S_n,m meets every prefix cylinder of length ≤n, so any chosen tail union is dense. Choose f_x(n) as the least m with S_n,m disjoint from ∪_(j≤n)F_j(x); the closed-code cylinder-hit predicate and least selection are Borel. Then H_x misses limsup S_n,f_x(n), while its complement is meagre. These pointwise and parameterized constructions give Borel cofinal master families exactly as claimed. The fixed countable standard codes and least-index selections use no new choice principle; Borel uniformity is proved by the two predecessor inductions, not inferred from pointwise selections.

references.title: Bartoszyński, Invariants of Measure and Category, §§2–3, printed pp.2–11

items.title: Transfer of null and meagre ideal invariants between Cantor space and the reals
items.statement: In ZFC, for each of the null and meagre ideals, the four cardinal invariants add, cov, non, and cof computed on Cantor space 2^ω equal the corresponding invariants on R, with the fair-coin measure on 2^ω and Lebesgue measure on R.
items.strategy: Remove from 2^ω the countable set of eventually constant binary sequences and from (0,1) the countable dyadic rationals. The binary-value map is then a homeomorphism between the remaining dense Gδ sets: finite digit agreement gives local continuity away from dyadic endpoints in both directions. The published fair-coin construction is the pushforward of Lebesgue measure under the inverse digit map, so this homeomorphism preserves the measure classes; the removed sets are both null and meagre. The published Cantor/Baire gap coding and irrationals/Baire homeomorphism provide an independent category check. Null and meagre subsets admit Borel null/meagre hulls, hence arbitrary ideal membership is preserved after deleting the countable exceptional sets. For a single global correspondence, partition R minus its countable set of integral translates of dyadic rationals into the clopen components (n,n+1) minus dyadics, n∈Z. Partition 2^ω minus its countable eventually-constant set into clopen components [0^k1] minus eventually-constant tails, k∈ω, and fix a bijection Z↔ω. The binary-value homeomorphism on each component, followed by its prefix 0^k1, gives a homeomorphism of the two disjoint-union cores; on each component its measure is scaled by a positive constant, so it preserves null sets as well as meagre sets. Countable unions across components preserve each sigma ideal. Extend this core bijection arbitrarily over the two countable exceptional sets. The resulting bijection of R with 2^ω preserves both ideals in both directions, since countable modifications are null and meagre. It therefore transports inclusion-cofinal bases, covers, nonideal witnesses and additivity witnesses exactly, proving all eight cardinal equalities without a cardinal-exponentiation assumption.

references.title: Bartoszyński, Invariants of Measure and Category, §§2–3, printed pp.2–11

items.title: Ideal Tukey morphisms control additivity and cofinality
items.statement: Let I,J be proper ideals whose add and cof minima are attained, and suppose maps u:I→J and v:J→I satisfy u(A)⊆B ⇒ A⊆v(B). Then add(J)≤add(I) and cof(I)≤cof(J). The same conclusion holds for cofinal master-code subfamilies in place of the full ideals.
items.strategy: If {A_i:i<κ}⊂I and κ<add(J), then ∪_i u(A_i) is contained in some B∈J, so every A_i⊂v(B) and ∪_i A_i∈I. Therefore κ<add(I), yielding add(J)≤add(I). If {B_j:j<cof(J)} is cofinal in J, then for any A∈I choose j with u(A)⊂B_j; the morphism gives A⊂v(B_j). Thus {v(B_j)} is cofinal in I and cof(I)≤cof(J). For cofinal master families, first replace arbitrary ideal members by a covering master member. This is Bartoszyński Lemma 2.2 with both inequality directions checked explicitly.

items.title: Null master codes and summable slaloms have both Tukey morphisms
items.statement: In ZFC, for the null master family N_f and the summable slalom order C from the preceding definition, there are Borel ideal-order morphisms N⪯C and C⪯N, with eventual inclusion as the slalom order.
items.strategy: For N⪯C, map a null code f to h_f(n)={f(2n),f(2n+1)}; this is a slalom since Σ2/2^n<∞. Given S∈C, form H_S=limsup_n ∪_{i∈S(n)}(C^(2n)_i ∪ C^(2n+1)_i). Its sections are null because the sum of their measures is bounded by a constant times Σ|S(n)|/2^n. The uniform Borel master-code lemma assigns a Borel null code g(S) covering H_S. If h_f⊂*S, then every point occurring infinitely often in f’s even or odd clopens lies in H_S⊂N_g(S), so N_f⊂N_g(S). For C⪯N, ignore the finitely many initial slalom coordinates and, for n≥1, allocate disjoint coordinate blocks of length n for independent clopen events G^n_i of measure 2^-n. For S∈C, the Borel family H_S=limsup_n ∪_{i∈S(n)}G^n_i is null by summability; take a Borel master code u(S) covering it. Given null code f, let F_m(f)=∩_{n≥m}(2^ω\C^n_f(n)); these closed sets increase to the conull complement of N_f. Borelly choose the least m with μ(F_m)>1/2, obtaining compact Kprime_f disjoint from N_f. Delete from Kprime_f every basic clopen U_j whose intersection with Kprime_f has measure zero. The remaining compact K_f has measure >1/2, is disjoint from N_f, depends Borelly on f via closed-section hit codes (for each clopen V, K_f∩V is nonempty iff every finite-stage closed deletion still meets V, by compactness), and every nonempty K_f∩U_j has positive measure. Define T_(f,j)(n)={i: K_f∩U_j≠∅ and K_f∩U_j∩G^n_i=∅}. If K_f∩U_j is nonempty, independence gives 0<μ(K_f∩U_j)≤∏_(n,i∈T_(f,j)(n))(1−2^-n), hence Σ_n |T_(f,j)(n)|/2^n<∞; if empty, take T_(f,j)(n)=∅. These slaloms depend Borelly on f. Borelly choose strictly increasing thresholds N_j≥j with Σ_(n≥N_j)|T_(f,j)(n)|/2^n<2^-j, and put T_f(n)=∪_{j:N_j≤n}T_(f,j)(n), making T_f∈C and T_(f,j)⊂*T_f for every j. If H_S⊂N_f, then compact K_f is covered by closed sets ∩_{n≥m}(2^ω\∪_{i∈S(n)}G^n_i). Baire category supplies a basic U_j meeting K_f on which all G^n_i with i∈S(n) are absent for n≥m. Thus S⊂*T_(f,j)⊂*T_f. This proves C⪯N with the exact direction used in Bartoszyński Lemma 3.13; the Borel master-code regrouping repairs its abbreviated first map. The slalom space C is Borel because summability is the countable union over integer bounds of the condition that every finite partial sum stays below that bound. The parameter spaces ω^ω and C are Borel-coded into the co-countable Gδ Cantor core by the published Cantor/Baire map; extend each Borel family by empty sections off its coded parameter domain before applying the uniform master-code lemma, then restrict the resulting Borel selector.

items.title: A good clopen family with finite intersections
items.statement: There is a Borel-coded array of clopen sets S^n_m in Cantor space and a repeating enumeration U_n of its basic clopen sets such that each S^n_m meets U_n, for every dense open U and n some S^n_m lies in U, and the intersection of any at most 2^n members of {S^n_m:m∈ω} is nonempty and meets U_n.
items.strategy: Enumerate all clopen sets as C_k, and repeat each basic clopen U infinitely often in the sequence U_n. For fixed n and k let A_k contain every l>k such that C_l∩U_n∩∩_{i∈I}C_i is nonempty whenever I⊂{0,…,k} and U_n∩∩_{i∈I}C_i is nonempty. For a dense open U, A_k contains arbitrarily late l with C_l⊂U: there are only finitely many nonempty clopen intersections to hit, and each meets U; choose a finite union of tiny clopen pieces inside U meeting them all, with arbitrarily many distinct choices. Let each S^n_m enumerate unions C_(m_0)∪…∪C_(m_q), q=2^n, with m_0 chosen so C_(m_0)∩U_n is nonempty and m_(i+1)∈A_(m_i). For the good-family condition choose C_(m_0) inside U∩U_n and each later C_(m_i) inside U; the A condition keeps the needed finite intersections nonempty, and the union lies in U. For the finite-intersection condition take q+1 such unions and reorder them greedily: choose first a row with least 0th index, then from the remaining rows one with least 1st index, and so on. The diagonal clopens C_(m_i^i), i≤q, have nonempty common intersection with U_n by induction. At step j every prior selected index is at most m_j^(j−1), while m_j^j∈A_(m_j^(j−1)), so the defining A property preserves the intersection. Since each diagonal clopen lies in its row union, the row unions intersect in U_n. This is the construction and orientation of Bartoszyński Lemma 3.15, with the finite diagonal induction explicit. All finite clopen choices can be made by least-index search in the fixed enumeration; no choice principle is used.

items.title: Meagre master codes Tukey-reduce to summable slaloms
items.statement: For the good clopen master family M_f and summable slalom order C, there are Borel maps witnessing M⪯C in the ideal-inclusion morphism sense.
items.strategy: The special good family is cofinal: for any meagre A⊂∪_j F_j with closed nowhere-dense F_j, choose S^n_f(n) inside the dense open complement of ∪_(j≤n)F_j; then A⊂M_f. For a meagre master code f in this family, put u(f)(n)={f(n)}; Σ_n 1/2^n<∞, so u(f)∈C. For S∈C, summability gives |S(n)|≤2^n for all sufficiently large n. Form W_n(S)=∩_{i∈S(n)}S^n_i, taking the whole space if S(n) is empty and ignoring the finitely many early exceptional n. The good-family finite-intersection lemma gives W_n(S)∩U_n≠∅ for all late n. Because the basis enumeration U_n repeats every basic clopen infinitely often, each tail union ∪_{n≥m}W_n(S) is dense open; hence L_S=2^ω\limsup W_n(S) is meagre. The family (S,y)↦[y∈L_S] is Borel because its clopen factors are finite and Borel in S. Apply the uniform Borel closed-nowhere-dense cover lemma to the Borel family L_S (after Cantor-coding its slalom parameter) to obtain Borel closed-section codes F_j(S) covering L_S. For each n choose v(S)(n) as the least m for which S^n_m is disjoint from ∪_(j≤n)F_j(S); the good-family property makes this possible, and clopen-versus-closed hit tests make v Borel. Then L_S⊂M_v(S) in this same special good-clopen family. If u(f)⊂*S, then S^n_f(n) contains W_n(S) for all late n, so M_f=2^ω\limsup S^n_f(n)⊂L_S⊂M_v(S). This is the exact M⪯C relation of Bartoszyński Lemma 3.14. The fixed enumerations and least-index choices are explicit and add no choice use beyond the ambient ideal framework. The slalom space C is Borel because summability is the countable union over integer bounds of the condition that every finite partial sum stays below that bound. The parameter spaces ω^ω and C are Borel-coded into the co-countable Gδ Cantor core by the published Cantor/Baire map; extend each Borel family by empty sections off its coded parameter domain before applying the uniform closed-cover lemma, then restrict the resulting Borel selector.

items.title: The null-to-meagre Tukey inequalities
items.statement: In ZFC, add(N)≤add(M) and cof(M)≤cof(N).

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: Compose the Borel morphism M⪯C from the good-clopen lemma with C⪯N from the independent-event/compact-positive-measure lemma to obtain M⪯N. Apply the ideal Tukey monotonicity lemma: add(N)≤add(M) and cof(M)≤cof(N), with no reversal of the morphism direction. The master-code families are cofinal, so their code-level morphism induces the full ideal inequalities. The Cantor-to-real transfer lemma identifies both ideals’ add and cof values with the values in the statement on R. The exact map constructions are in the two predecessor lemmas and Bartoszyński Lemmas 3.13–3.15; the cardinal and measure conventions inherit their stated ZFC background, while the fixed enumerations and least-code choices add no choice use.

items.title: Cross-ideal and eventual-domination arrows of Cichoń’s diagram
items.statement: In ZFC, cov(N)≤non(M), cov(M)≤non(N), add(M)≤b≤non(M), and cov(M)≤d≤cof(M).

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: First construct a dense null Gδ set B⊂R: for each n cover the rationals by a dense open union O_n of intervals of total length <2^-n, and put B=∩_n O_n. Its complement C is meagre. If X is nonmeagre, every translate y−B is comeagre and meets X; the null translates {x+B:x∈X} cover R, proving cov(N)≤non(M). If X is nonnull, every translate y−C is conull and meets X; the meagre translates {x+C:x∈X} cover R, proving cov(M)≤non(N). For category arrows pass between R modulo Q and Cantor space modulo the countable dense set D of eventually-zero sequences: R minus Q≅ω^ω by the published homeomorphism, and 2^ω minus D≅ω^ω by successive gaps between 1s. Countable omitted sets are meagre and do not change the four uncountable meagre invariants. In ω^ω, B_g={x:x≤*g} is meagre and dominates every family of size <b, yielding b≤non(M); a dominating family of size d gives a meagre cover, yielding cov(M)≤d. For the remaining arrows work in 2^ω. For each n enumerate every finite interval cylinder [s] on coordinates [n,k), k>n. These form a good family: any dense open U contains one such cylinder, by finitely processing the 2^n prefixes and extending a common tail string; every such cylinder meets every prefix cylinder of length ≤n. For f choosing one interval cylinder S_n(f(n)) at each n, put M_f=2^ω minus limsup_n S_n(f(n)); this is meagre because each tail union is dense open. The family {M_f} is inclusion-cofinal in the meagre ideal: given A⊂∪_j F_j with F_j closed nowhere dense, choose S_n(f(n)) inside the dense open complement of ∪_{j≤n}F_j, so A∩limsup S_n(f(n))=∅. Let k_f(n) be the right endpoint of S_n(f(n)). For strictly increasing g with g(n)>n put E_g={x: eventually every interval [n,g(n)) contains a 1}; E_g is meagre, since the limsup of the zero-block cylinders is comeagre. If g(n)>k_f(n) infinitely often, thin these n to disjoint [n,g(n)) intervals, assign x|[n,k_f(n)) the prescribed S_n(f(n)) patterns, and assign 1 elsewhere. Then x∈E_g but x∉M_f: inside each prescribed zero run the coordinate k_f(n)<g(n) is 1, while outside prescribed blocks x itself is 1. Thus E_g⊆M_f implies g≤*k_f. If a family {E_g:g∈G} with G unbounded of size b had meagre union, one cofinal M_f would contain it and k_f would dominate G, contradiction; hence add(M)≤b. If {A_i:i<cof(M)} is an inclusion-cofinal meagre basis, choose f_i with A_i⊆M_f_i. Every E_g lies in some A_i, so g≤*k_f_i, making {k_f_i} dominating and proving d≤cof(M). The source's chopped-real map is reconstructed here with explicit witness orientation. AC selects the witness families and codes.

items.title: Cichoń’s diagram inequalities
items.statement: In ZFC, the ten entries add(N),cov(N),non(N),cof(N),add(M),cov(M),non(M),cof(M),b,d satisfy the standard Cichoń diagram: the elementary ideal arrows and the null-to-meagre, cross-ideal and eventual-domination arrows in the preceding lemmas, together with their transitive consequences. No independence or completeness claim is included.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: The ideal lemma supplies add(I)≤cov(I), add(I)≤non(I), cov(I)≤cof(I), non(I)≤cof(I) for I=N,M. The Tukey lemma supplies add(N)≤add(M) and cof(M)≤cof(N). The cross/bounding lemma supplies cov(N)≤non(M), cov(M)≤non(N), add(M)≤b≤non(M), and cov(M)≤d≤cof(M). The basic b,d lemma supplies b≤d. Draw precisely these generating arrows on the ten named nodes, close only under transitivity, and compare with Bartoszyński Theorem 3.11; this yields the standard Cichoń diagram asserted, without an independence or missing-arrow claim. AC enters through the supplier cardinal minima and maps.

items.title: ZFC does not determine the continuum function
items.statement: False: ZFC fixes the value of 2^κ for every infinite regular κ.
items.strategy: Start with the GCH relative-consistency result. At κ=ℵ1 use published Add(ℵ1,ℵ3), which preserves cardinals and forces 2^ℵ1=ℵ3, while GCH has 2^ℵ1=ℵ2. State the external finite-fragment consistency interpretation and do not infer the existence of an external transitive model from Con(ZFC). AC is used in both forcing computations.

title: Easton's Theorem and Cardinal Invariants of the Continuum: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A diagonal pseudointersection of a countable tower prefix
items.statement: For any sequence A_0⊇*A_1⊇*⋯ of infinite subsets of ω, construct an explicit increasing x_n in ⋂_{i≤n}A_i; the set X={x_n:n<ω} is a pseudointersection.
items.strategy: Finite intersections are infinite because A_n differs from earlier A_i only finitely. Choose x_n strictly above x_{n-1} in that finite intersection. For each i, all x_n with n≥i lie in A_i.

items.title: Under CH the listed classical invariants equal aleph one
items.statement: In ZFC, assuming CH, p,t,b,d,s,r and the eight add/cov/non/cof values for N and M all equal ℵ1.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: Each invariant is at least ℵ1 by countable diagonalization or countable ideal closure and at most c by its defining witness and Borel bases. Under CH c=ℵ1. For s and r prove the countable lower bound directly from diagonalization if the comparison lemma remains escalated. AC is used to identify all minima as cardinals.

items.title: A two-coordinate Easton pattern
items.statement: Over GCH, prescribe F(ℵ0)=ℵ3 and F(ℵ1)=ℵ3 on the two regular cardinals ℵ0,ℵ1. The set-sized Easton product preserves cardinals and gives 2^ℵ0=2^ℵ1=ℵ3.
items.strategy: Check monotonicity and cf(ℵ3)=ℵ3>ℵ1. Apply the set-sized realization theorem at both coordinates; no singular value is asserted.

items.title: MA iteration computes null and meagre additivity
items.statement: In the published ω2-length MA iteration over GCH, c=ℵ2 and add(N)=add(M)=ℵ2.

references.title: Bartoszynski, Invariants of Measure and Category

items.strategy: The iteration forces MA and c=ℵ2. Published MA consequences make every union of <c null or meagre sets remain in the corresponding ideal, so add(N),add(M)≥c. The singleton cover of all reals gives the reverse inequality. AC is used in the published iteration and cardinal calculation.
